Pompous

POM-pus -- stress on the first syllable, POM. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Pompous is irritatingly self-important or grand.

The pompous professor referred to his own weekly lectures as 'historic events.'

Worked Example

The host of the school awards night spends ten minutes describing his own trophies, adjusts his medal twice, and only then remembers to announce the actual winner.

That inflated self-display is pompous: treating oneself as grand and important in a way that makes everyone else roll their eyes. Pompous behavior is not just pride -- it is pride performed for an audience.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

self-important: having an inflated sense of one's own value

arrogant: overbearingly proud and superior

grandiose: impressively showy far beyond what is justified

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

humble: modest about one's own importance

unassuming: not drawing attention to oneself

Where it sits · how puffed up the display is — self-important → pompous → grandiose

self-important vs. pompous: Self-important is the plainer, milder label -- a self-important person overrates their own value, while a pompous one puts that inflated self on parade, complete with grand words and ceremony.

grandiose vs. pompous: Grandiose swells even beyond pompous: a pompous speaker inflates himself in front of a room, while a grandiose plan or manner balloons past all reality, promising palaces where a shed would do.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — pomp-

root — pomp-: procession; splendid display (Greek pompe 'procession, display,' via Latin pompa)

suffix — -ous

suffix — -ous: full of; possessing the qualities of (Latin -osus, via Old French -ous)

Put it together

Put it together: Pompous uses the -ous variant of this unit's suffix family. Greek pompe was a grand procession -- banners, trumpets, display -- so pompous literally means 'full of pomp': a person who turns ordinary life into a parade in their own honor.

Use the root in a new word: pomp

Use the root in a new word: pomp: The coronation's pomp included trumpets, silk banners, and a golden carriage.

Root Check

Word Choice

Pompous is always a criticism -- it mocks the gap between how grand people act and how grand they actually are. It loves company with speech: a pompous tone, a pompous announcement, pompous titles. Genuine dignity is never pompous; the word marks dignity that is performed.
